Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance, perhaps I could put my first question to the Prime Minister.
Two days ago I asked the Prime Minister a question concerning our current account deficit of $5.2 billion; in other words, our shortfall with the outside world-$5.2 billion being a record for this country. At that time the Prime Minister hesitated to reply. Could he tell the House, first, has he looked into these figures; second, has he had discussions with his Minister of Finance; and third, does he agree with the Minister of Finance that it is a problem we will simply have to live with?
March 9, 1979

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
"No" to the first two questions, Mr. Speaker, and "Yes" to the third.
S)

Can the Prime Minister go further and tell us what, specifically, he sees the government doing to relieve the situation, bearing in mind that the current account deficit means our dollar will stay under heavy pressure? This causes inflation in the country. For example, we find that raw hide prices in Canada went from 42 cents a pound to $1.05 a pound this week. This is largely due to the fact that Japanese and Korean buyers find that our hides are now so cheap that they are reaching over, buying them and driving up Canadian domestic prices, with the result that shoe prices, already up this spring $2 to $3 a pair, will be up substantially more come the fall.
We'll all be barefoot.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has been a capital importing nation for many, many decades. We continue to be a capital importing nation. The essential question is whether this creates development in Canada, creates jobs and creates expansion. This has been the history of the past half century, that foreign capital has added itself to Canadian savings in order to develop this country. I have never heard any party protest against that, including the party of the hon. member.

The Prime Minister apparently misses the question. The fact is we are paying for last year's grocery bills; we are paying what we owe the rest of the world. This is not bringing in capital to build the infrastructure of this country. As a result, we have a low dollar which has now caused oranges, for example, to go from $1.78 to $2.28, a 28 per cent increase compared to last March. The same is true of various other products: grapefruit have gone from 25 cents to 33 cents each, up 28 per cent due to the inadequacy of this government's fiscal policy.
Will the Prime Minister now tell the House that he made a mistake in the past and that he is going to bring in proper fiscal measures to arrest this haemorrhaging compared with the rest of the world?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know if I will manage to explain it to the hon. member. If people want to buy oranges, grapefruit and bananas, they will have to pay the price for them that is set in other countries.
Oh, oh!
Let them eat cake!

Cake can be made in our country. I know the hon. member's face is full of it all the time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister. This morning he spoke about the cost of imported goods which has increased because of the drop in value of the dollar. The same kind of increases have occurred with regard to Canadian-produced goods. Sockeye salmon went up over 23 per cent in the last year. My colleague mentioned the increase in price of raw hides.
Does the government have any plan to take fiscal steps to correct these increasing price levels and inflation, or are all these price increases simply something the Canadian people will have to live with?

subsubtopic: NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION-MANNER OF OPERATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Prime Minister with regard to the National Commission on Inflation. How can the government expect the commission to be successful if it is given no guidelines to appraise price performance in the economy?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION-MANNER OF OPERATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the mandate given to the commission is to watch for any settlements or increases in incomes or prices which would be dangerous in causing accelerated inflation. That is a matter of judgment. Mr. Renouf and his commissioners will exercise their judgment ably in the future as they have in the past.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION-MANNER OF OPERATION
speechtext: In that case, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government itself has any guidelines which it will use in making its own judgments on the reports from this commission. How will the government determine what constitutes normal price, wage and profit behaviour, and how will it determine what constitutes abnormal or reprehensible behaviour in this area?

subsubtopic: NATIONAL COMMISSION ON INFLATION-MANNER OF OPERATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this kind of judgment is made all the time by people engaged, for instance, in collective bargaining. When you refer to an arbitrator, you do not give him guidelines. You ask him to look at what would be an appropriate settlement in a particular case. He looks at settlements in other areas. He considers whether there is need for a catch-up or whether the group involved is ahead of others, and he makes a judgment. The same thing can be done with regard to prices.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Before the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity was aborted by the government, it made public a number of significant findings concerning the cost of living in Canada. For example, it pointed to food industry profits and dairy industry costs, and criticized the government's wage settlement with letter carriers as being excessive and inflationary.
March 9, 1979

What action will be taken to follow up on these findings, and what about the many other studies CSIP was undertaking? Will they be published, or will they also be aborted?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has given examples to his colleague from Ottawa of the kind of judgment which can be made without any specific guidelines. I hope these new members will meet and explain some things to each other.
Why don't you answer the question?

Mr. Speaker, in introducing the National Commission on Inflation last Friday, the Minister of Finance claimed it would have broader investigatory powers than CSIP and that this would enable the commission to get to the truth behind rising prices. I understand that when CSIP requested information from companies, only a very few refused to provide it; and I am pleased to hear that the minister is concerned about the truth. It is in this regard that I put my supplementary question. Why is the NCI not directly responsible to parliament, as CSIP was, and why is the NCI reporting to the minister and not to parliament and the people of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, CSIP was under the direction of the Economic Council of Canada which was not reporting directly to parliament; it was reporting directly to the Prime Minister. The new group will report to the Minister of Finance. I do not think there is any objection to that, even on the part of the hon. member.
The important thing is that in the case of CSIP it was put under the Economic Council of Canada at the request of the provinces which, at the time we were discussing the post-controls period, did not want that particular institution to have any power to compel production of information. Experience has shown that that was not sufficient because some groups did, indeed, refuse to supply CSIP with information. That is why we took the next step.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Parliament can only operate properly if questions asked in parliament are answered within a reasonable period of time.
Yesterday Your Honour made a ruling that he had taken a certain step because of the fact that a committee of this House had made the recommendations as to the guidelines, and therefore he took it upon himself to decide that certain broadcasts should not take place. I mention that because through the years parliament, over and over again, has declared both effectively and traditionally that there shall not be unreasonable delays in the answering of questions.
I brought this matter to Your Honour's attention a couple of weeks ago and you very properly said that you had no authority to take any action but that you would look into the question. What I am dealing with is, to me, one of the most reprehensible examples on the part of the government of its efforts to hide the facts. I brought this matter to the attention

March 9, 1979
Point of Order-Mr. Diefenbaker
of the House several weeks ago. Since then there has been no action thereon and I must therefore repeat once more the questions that were asked three and a half months ago.
Question No. 576 placed on the order paper on November 14 reads as follows:
1.	Was an order made that files containing secret or security information were not to be released until the expiry of 30 years and, if so, on what date?
There was such an order and date. I have it at the moment. The question continues:
2.	Has the government decided that all files in connection with the Gouzenko revelations of 1945-46 shall not be released now and, if so, for what reason and on what basis?
3.	Is the government aware of a press report that the reason given for non-production is "That they might hurt some people now living"?
4.	Were any such individuals then or thereafter or since Cabinet Ministers?
Another question, No. 611, was asked in connection therewith on November 22 as follows:
1.	In consequence of Mr. Igor Gouzenko's revelations, how many individuals were prosecuted and (a) who were they (b) what happened in their respective cases?
2.	How many named in the revelations were not prosecuted and for what reason?
3.	With the termination of the 30 years during which secret documents are not revealed, for what reason is an exception being made in connection with his revelations?
Sir, I have been here a long while, almost 39 years, and I have never known a case to equal this in which concealment is the obvious purpose of the government in not answering. What is the reason for the concealment? They are very simple questions. Parliament becomes effete unless answers are given to questions within a reasonable time.
In addition, I asked a question on February 6, No. 1,032 on the order paper, as follows:
1.	Did the government give its consent to the Government of France to confer on Dr. William Jaffe the Legion d'Honneur and, if so, on what date?
2.	Did the government give its consent to the granting of the Award, some time ago, of Chevalier of the Order of the Legion d'Honneur on Premier Levesque and, if so, on what date?
Why was that question not answered? It is not a long delay, only a month, but it would take about five minutes to answer if the government desired to answer it.
I endeavoured to have you, sir, as custodian of the traditions of parliament, as you made clear yesterday, to do something and you said nothing could be done. Why is this government hiding information? It has been three and a half or almost four months since these questions went on the order paper. What are they afraid of? There can be no excuse whatever for this kind of Star Chamber action.
We approach an election, I believe, at some time. Why have members of this government who posed as lambs now become rabbits when it comes to answering simple questions? Who is covering up? I repeat-you cannot do anything, you have made that clear-the House and the country has the right to know that the failure to answer these questions in three and a half months indicates a government that cannot be believed. That is what we have found here over and over again.

This is an example of simple questions that could be answered. Is the government waiting for dissolution? How many months do we have to wait? Are they waiting to allow this session of parliament to end because they have no reason to believe they are frightened of the answers if they are given to the Canadian people?

Mr. Speaker, what I find unacceptable in the remarks of the right hon. member is his insinuations to the effect that we, on this side of the House, have something to hide, while in fact our attitude proves quite the contrary. If I may refresh the memory of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), in the last two sessions we answered, to my knowledge, about 90 per cent of the thousands of questions put on the order paper. In so doing we also try to get maximum information. 1 see the right hon. member is not interested in knowing the facts; yet he complains about our hiding them, Mr. Speaker. There he goes making gestures which would indicate that he is not interested in knowing the truth about the matter. I am giving him the information requested and I ask him to have the decency and politeness to listen.
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. member knows full well that during a session, when we try on this side of the House to get all the information and give answers that are as complete as possible, we manage to keep up a 39 to 42 per cent rate of reply. Then, during the summer recess, we usually manage to give answers to about another 40 per cent of the questions on the order paper so that, come fall, towards the end of September or in October, when the new session starts, we have by then answered 90 per cent of all questions on the order paper.
The right hon. member should know that an average of some 4,000 to 5,000 questions are listed each year on the order paper. He should also know that of those, several are referred to dozens or even some forty departments or government agencies and that each question that is so channelled costs,

today, in 1979, in this day and age, an average of $100 each to every agency or department concerned.
I have always maintained in this House, however, that it is not a matter of money or of judging whether the question of the hon. member is stupid or not. We treat all questions on the same footing. As they are put, they are referred to the departments and agencies concerned, and as soon as we get all the information requested, we answer them. Everyday, I answer some question or other on the order paper and we print them without discrimination.
The right hon. member should know that what he is trying to do today is unfair to his colleagues on both sides of the House. It is unfair to stand in this House and bring up the matter every two or three weeks. He has just done so now, and did it three weeks ago. He had three questions put on the order paper which bore an asterisk as our standing orders allow. We have already answered one third of those questions. We answered his question bearing an asterisk about fifteen days or less than two weeks ago.
There are two other starred questions and we are dealing with them seriously. Mr. Speaker, if other hon. members did not respect this institution more than he does and if we had to rise every day to read questions on the order paper, the House would continuously hear the same thing. We can read them in the order paper. We do the necessary research work, we give the answers, and each hon. member is put on an equal footing. I have deep respect for the right hon. member for Prince Albert but I have as much respect for the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard) who is here or for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Everybody here is put on an equal footing. There is no preference. Each question is considered seriously. Once again, finally, I hope that the right hon. member will understand that we have nothing to hide. We showed in the last few years that we answer 90 per cent of the questions on the order paper, which demonstrates the very opposite of the innuendos of the right hon. member for Prince Albert, which are unfounded.
I take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to tell the right hon. member, once and for all, in a very polite and respectful manner, in reply to his point of order, that he is complaining of certain anomalies in the standing orders. I once told him, about two years ago, that he was complaining about 1/116th of the problems we are faced with in this House. There are 116 House standing orders, Mr. Speaker. There is a need here for an in-depth revision not only of one rule but of all the standing orders of this House. If he and his party seriously wished to sit down and discuss the changes required to modernize this institution and make it more efficient, I would be the first to support his efforts. But as long as he behaves in this manner, wasting our time by reading his own questions on the order paper, complaining without reason and insinuating that we, on this side of the House, are seeking to hide the truth, I cannot consider that he is acting in good faith and it would be very

difficult for me to sit down with him in a positive attempt to reform this institution in such a way that it would reflect our times, prove to be more efficient and give a new meaning to our role as members of parliament.

speakeroldname: Mr. Louis Duclos (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
1. The Bureau of International Cultural Relations in the Department of External Affairs was created as a distinct entity to reflect the increasing importance attached to projecting Canada's cultural image abroad in support of Canadian foreign policy objectives. As is the case for all bureaux in the department, the Bureau of International Cultural Relations reports through the Under-Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
2.	The Bureau of International Cultural Relations is comprised of the academic relations division, cultural affairs division and historical division, all of which formerly formed part of the Bureau of Public Affairs. The new bureau will not be taking over the responsibilities of any other programs. Its relationship with Canadian missions abroad will continue to be one of close co-operation in promoting Canada's cultural image abroad.
3.	Mr. Gilles Lefebvre has been appointed to the new bureau. Formerly director of the Canadian Cultural Centre in Paris he studied music in Ottawa and Paris and gained an international reputation for his work with "Jeunesses musica-les du Canada", which he founded in 1949, and the Orford Arts Centre which he also established. He has served five terms as president of the "Federation internationale des jeunesses musicales" (36 countries are members) and was president of the Canadian Conference of the Arts from 1970 to
1972.	His responsibilities will be those of director general of the bureau.
4.	No programs were abolished. The creation of the new Bureau of International Cultural Relations does not represent any reduction in the annual budget of the Department of External Affairs.

speechtext: At the beginning of the discussion on clause 1 I should like to say I very much appreciate the co-operation which has been extended to me by the housing critic for the official opposition, by the housing critic for the New Democratic Party and by the hon. member for Bellechasse. A year ago last February, I think it was, the minister met with the provinces and outlined changes he thought should take place in the National Housing Act. Hon. members will recall that last April there was a scare, or mini-scare, about an election. At that point certain pronouncements were made. We waited to see what would happen; we hoped legislation would be brought before the House. I think it was last November or December that we heard there were to be changes. Again we waited. History has shown that when we go through the proper procedures with respect to a bill we usually get a good piece of

legislation. I must say I feel very sad we are not able to consider this measure in the standing committee following second reading. I do not like to be negative after all the good times we have had in the last two days, but there are three things which concern our side very greatly.
Housing has not been a priority of this government or this situation would not have arisen. I refer to the fact that we are suddenly obliged to forgo committee meetings on this important subject. We on our side wanted these committee meetings very much.
Mr. Chairman, there are three things we wanted, to discuss. We wanted to discuss this whole graduated mortgage payments system. We think this is a departure from what we would have done.
We had hoped that in committee we could have studied AHOP, which was a good program. We felt that some things should have been studied so that we could find out why there has been a high default rate recently. I feel very sad that we could not bring in witnesses and that we could not have the time to find out what happened to AHOP.
We had hoped to study the good parts and the weak parts of the program in relation to this new program. Even yesterday all members of the House received a booklet put out by the ministry with respect to the graduated mortgage payment, as if it already was approved. We have not even had time to discuss it. I am new in this area, but I come from a management background and the most important thing about putting out a new product is that it be test-marketed. Products should be evaluated. There should not be mass distribution of something until it has been analysed.
I am worried because we did not spend some time after second reading having proper committee meetings. There are some very fine experts we on this side wanted to bring in. I do not think that is right. I recognize that the minister has politics on his mind, and I understand that. I have had politics on my mind this week too, but I say that the graduated mortgage payment really should have been studied.
We on this side have a few amendments to move. My amendment is about housing projects, and part of my amendment reads as follows:
-"housing project" means a project consisting of one or more houses, one or more multiple-family dwellings, housing acommodation of the hostel or dormitory type, two or more condominium units or any combination thereof, together with any public space, recreational facilities, commercial space and other buildings appropriate to the project, but does not include a hotel;-

happen to feel that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has had a very fine and admirable reputation over the years.

My colleague, the hon. member for Selkirk, will be speaking about another amendment. One of our amendments deals with tragic AHOP cases regarding quality problems. Mr. Chairman, it has been said that nothing concentrates the mind of a man more than the prospect of hanging. I can say, with respect to this bill, that nothing has so concentrated the mind of the minister as the prospect of an election.
That being said, I want to join in the sugary part of these proceedings by saying that I appreciate the courtesy which has been offered to me and to people in my office as a result of the amendments which we intended to make and the efforts which the minister has made to have them incorporated in the bill.

I do not want to make a lengthy speech because we have agreed to certain limitations with respect to time, but I do want to emphasize that we in this party lament the tendency on the part of the government to allow its housing policy to become an insurance policy. We lament the fact that the Department of Urban Affairs has been abolished and, as I said in the committee some three months ago, it seemed to us that at a time when more and more Canadians were being confronted with problems in urban areas it was the height of irresponsibility for the government to abandon that critical field.
That being said, we do not agree with the basic thrust of the policies of the government. We recognize the importance, in the face of the legislation that has been put forward, of attempting to be as constructive as possible. The efforts we have made have really been twofold. First of all, we have tried to provide for the possibility, at least, of land assembly programs being continued by our municipalities and provinces by allowing the federal government to guarantee certain loans. We regret the fact that the government has abandoned its land assembly grants program to municipalities. We know for a fact that this has affected the ability of many of our city governments to put an end to land speculation and to construct housing on their own.
The second major thrust of our amendments which we will be putting forward later in the day has to do with taking out the statutory monetary limitation that is currently in the bill on the community service grants program. We think, as a matter of principle, it is a mistake for the government to have limited the amount of money to $250 million. When you include the loan portion that is currently available under NIP grants, you find there is no comparison between the government's efforts made under the community service grants program and the efforts previously made under previous divergent programs.
The over-all impact of the community service grants program will be that fewer funds rather than more funds will be allocated, not only for improvement of neighbourhoods but also for the construction of sewage projects, and so on. Therefore, we have argued that the monetary limits should be taken out and made subject to a review which it will be possible for the government to carry on, one that other governments could carry on in the event that other people are sitting on that side of the House, which, it seems to me, provides for the kind of flexibility we need.
I do not think there is any need to make a long speech. We indicated our views at length on second reading and so has the Conservative party. We take issue with the Conservative party's basic position on housing and we also take issue with the Liberal party's position on housing. As we enter the election period, it is perhaps best to leave it to Canadians to decide whose policy makes the most sense.

Mr. Chairman, here we are on March 9, in the House of Commons in committee of the whole, with that great spirit of co-operation and agreement. Today we feel that the minister, my colleague from Ottawa-Carleton, my col-

league from Broadview and I could go down to the United Nations and solve their problems and reach an agreement in that spirit of co-operation. That is the spirit in the House today, and it is reflected by the sunshine on this, the warmest and nicest day we have had here in Ottawa in four months.
However, there still remain sharp differences between the Liberal approach to housing and urban affairs, the approach of members in the P.C. party and certainly that of the NDP. But I want to point out to the minister and to hon. members here what we on this side are giving up, in this spirit of co-operation, to get this bill passed. We are also giving up the chance to query the minister in committee on why the government has decided to wind down the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. We agree that it is a good idea, one that we on this side have advocated, but we are still giving up the chance of putting questions to the minister.
Last night before I dropped off to sleep I was doing some light reading of Hansard and went back to a speech given on October 22, 1970 in this very chamber by the then minister of state for urban affairs.
Who was he then?

He is now the super minister, the present President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers. I was reading some of the comments he made when the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs was first created. Back in those days he was just a "clerk", a "reporter;" now he has come out of the telephone booth. He said at that time:
Let me repeat the words I have just used-consult, co-operate, co-ordinate. They are, in fact, precise indicators of how we will approach the problems posed by rapid urbanization in Canada at the federal level,
If I had time to read his speech I would show that his approach is like one who is found sniffing the thin air surrounding the metaphysical peaks of political intellectualism because he never deals with the centricity of the issue. It is a great speech.

speechtext: Order, please. When the House rose at one o'clock, the hon. member for Selkirk had the floor.

Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned for lunch at one o'clock I was quoting from the comments of the hon. member for Port Arthur as reported in Commons Debates for October 22, 1970. He was talking about the very first Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. Now that I have had some lunch, I return strengthened, encouraged and ready to quote again from this very eloquent speech. The speech was made approximately nine years ago, and it outlined the reasons why the then government was setting up the new Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. Of course, we have the same government today. It is long in the tooth, worn and weary, running down and will soon run out. But nine years ago it was a reasonably new government which was ready to work.
I should like to quote one other sentence from that speech in order to provide the committee with some idea of the hopes and dreams of the government at that time. At page 467 of Hansard the speech reads as follows:
We will hope to attract the best minds now diffused through governments, industries and universities and to return them again to governments, universities and industry in a continuous and cross-fertilizing stream.
That was a most noble objective, but I should like to deal with the crux, meat, essence and undergirding principle to establish the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. He went on
to say:
In addition to an urban secretariat, of course, the ministry shall have reporting to it, an increasingly co-ordinated into a more total urban effort, the Crown agencies, of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the National Capital Commission.
The minister then talked about setting up a senior interdepartmental committee to study, co-ordinate and to report annually to the minister. That committee was known as SIDCUA. The only problem with that committee was that it was not only made up of boys from the mail room but comprised of no less than deputy ministers of this government. These nine deputy ministers were to meet, co-ordinate, consult and determine whether or not the Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Urban Affairs was doing his job of co-ordinating the activities that would touch the provinces and the municipalities in order to maintain the jurisdictional argument and the constitutionality of rights respecting the provinces.
Those deputy ministers were not just put there for window dressing. They were in fact the backbone of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. So back in 1970 when this government introduced the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs they said that this most critical body of deputy ministers from some nine departments will make sure that this ministry is a coordinating ministry.

March 9, 1979
Housing
Let us look at the record. This committee made only one report in nine years. It was the first and only report. Now we have the minister and his government coming before the Canadian people and saying, "we want to wind down the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. It isn't working, we're stepping on the toes of the provinces, we're interfering with the municipalities. We are so sorry; after nine years of interfering with the provinces we want out."
They only took your advice.
Well, now, we have heard from my friend on the left who says that the government has taken our advice.
Like Saskatchewan took our advice on mortgage interest deductibility.

If I thought that this government would take my advice so readily, I would give them a list, and we would not only clean up the bill, we would clean up the government. If this government wishes to take my advice and the advice of most Canadians, it is that the Prime Minister ought to have more than lunch with the Governor General and that he should, indeed, ask for a writ so that the Canadian people can review the activities of this government which has been around here for some ten years. Nine of those ten years have been too long.
This government, Mr. Chairman, created the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. The ministry was to be reviewed by SIDCUA. We now have them coming back and saying that it did not work. We on this side wanted the ministry of state wound down because it was not working, not because the terms of reference were not adequate, but because this government went beyond the terms of reference. This government began to do things which were constitutionally within the bounds of the provinces.
As a matter of fact, the last task force of the western premiers, in a document known as "The Western Premiers' Task Force on Constitutional Trends", at page 31 says:
-in the broad area of housing, consultation was non-existent.
The four western premiers were saying that in fact the very duty of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs was non-existent. It is no wonder that we on this side say that the whole ministry of urban affairs should be wound down because housing is a provincial jurisdiction.
This, however, does not mean that the federal government does not have a role in housing. It does not mean that the federal government cannot co-operate with the provinces. The problem is that this government cannot co-operate with anybody. They cannot consult with anybody. Their concept of consultation is ratification. I will tell you, Mr. Chairman, how much they consult. This little booklet which I have will prove and illustrate the difference between consultation and ratification.
The historic role of parliament has been that the government proposes legislation, and I give them that right. They have the right to govern because they have the majority, for

the time being at least. They have the right to set the fiscal and monetary policy regardless of the mess they have made of it. That is their right and I give it to them. They have the right to set foreign affairs policy and housing policy, and I give it to them.
Our right in this House as the opposition is to oppose and to suggest from time to time alternatives that will help make legislation bearable for Canadians. The proof of this is illustrated in the number of amendments which we on this side have introduced on Bill C-29 which have been accepted by this government. This proves that we on this side are ready at the drop of a hat to help write legislation which will work. We on this side have the absolute right to oppose.
Another historic right of parliament is to debate proposals by the government before they are put into effect. I had delivered to my office down there in the "bush", in the Confederation building-but the post office was able to find me-a booklet that has printed on the back of it "NHA 522" and printed in the ninth month of 1978. This booklet is about graduated payment mortgages, "another way to home ownership". It was printed by the hundreds and thousands, and it says so right here. The cover letter says that over 100,000 copies of this booklet are available. All one has to do, Mr. Chairman, is fill out this card on the back; it is perforated and you tear it off and send it to CMHC; then they will send you this booklet outlining the graduated payment mortgage, the GPM.
However, the GPM is not law yet. It has not been passed. We have not given our consent. The difference is that this government comes to parliament for ratification when historically it should come to parliament for debate and approval of legislation. This government is so quick off the mark that they print 100,000 of these booklets. Just the day before yesterday the minister was prepared to scrap the GPM. It was only through amendments from this side that it was cleaned up. We did not want to see it scrapped, we wanted to make it workable. We introduced amendments which were accepted by the government and we would have saved the GPM and, in turn, the Canadian taxpayers the cost of printing 100,000 of these booklets before parliament had a chance to debate the question and help the government clean up the mess.
Maybe they are already printed.
They are, 100,000 of them.
At what cost?

At what cost? This government is not concerned with cost. What we on this side are forgoing is the chance to have this bill go to a standing committee where it would be investigated and where witnesses would be called from across the country, from, for example, the banking institutions and the credit unions, to give us their expert advice which is available to all Canadians. I have another problem, Mr. Chairman, that I spoke about the other evening. That is the problem in Kilbride in the district of St. John's West where some mistakes occurred through the administration by CMHC of an AHOP project there. I am not sure yet how many people are affected- perhaps 150.
To summarize the matter, in January all these people got notice that they were going to have an increased monthly mortgage payment. In some cases it was up to $80 per month. It was said the reason was that the municipal taxes had increased, or that it was to collect municipal taxes that had not been collected by CMHC in the previous two of three years. The increased monthly payments are to commence on April 1 and CMHC has said they will collect the arrears of taxes in 1979.
In some cases, Mr. Chairman, people had been told a few months earlier that they were in credit. In one case the monthly payments for municipal taxes were reduced to zero or to 50 cents per month, I think. That particular person has been told the monthly payments are to be increased to $40 or $50 per month because there are supposed to be arrears. Naturally the people who got these notices were shocked and stunned. They had never heard of any arrears of municipal taxes. They are objecting and meetings have been arranged so that CMHC can go into each individual case.
There was no tax increase in the last three years in the St. John's metropolitan area and there was no increase in tax assessments. CMHC had considered that taxes were going to be between $96 and $120 per year originally, but when the actual tax bills were sent out they were more than that. For some reason CMHC neglected to inform the mortgagors. They neglected to increase the mortgage payments for municipal taxes, then allowed the arrears to build up over two or three years which they paid themselves. They now want to collect the arrears from the mortgagors. They want to collect the interest on the arrears, and they want to do this all in nine months commencing April 1.
Mr. Chairman, that is not acceptable. These are low income people, working class people or lower middle income people who cannot afford to pay vastly increased monthly payments.

CMHC is aware of the situation in St. John's. We have been talking to them, but they need direction from the minister, as I said in that speech.
Without going on too long about that, I would like to know what the minister can do. First I hope he will direct that they will not collect arrears of interest on municipal taxes which the mortgagors know nothing about. They were not informed about this matter and it is not their fault. There should be no collection of arrears. Depending on the individual case, people should have longer that 12 months to pay the arrears, once the arrears are shown to exist. There should be no attempt to collect arrears of interest caused by CMHC making late payments of municipal taxes to the St. John's metropolitan area board.
Apparently CMHC were charged interest by the St. John's metropolitan area board because they did not pay the taxes themselves on time, and they were in turn trying to collect that from these mortgagors. It may be something to do with the computers. Anyway, it was some fault in the administrative system of CMHC, and as a result this happened.
This situation is the responsibility of CMHC, and I cannot see how these people can be expected to start paying on April 1. It will take two or three months to straighten this matter out. CMHC should be directed not to start collecting their increased monthly payments until at least June 1 or until this matter has been straightened out with these very irate home owners.
It was not drawn to my attention until all this happened that many of the homes occupied by these AHOP home owners- once again built by a contractor through CMHC, inspected by CMHC and all the rest of it, and then sold to these poor innocents-are defective. They have had a lot of trouble with them. They are in poor repair already although they have only been built in the last two or three years. The workmanship is atrocious. The roofs leak. There is condensation inside and outside the walls. I am told that they have things growing literally on the walls of their houses. I do not know what kinds of things. There is water everywhere.
Fungus.
There is some evidence of NDP fungus.
A healthy development.
I am afraid not. It will require the absolute excavation of these structures if that turns out to be true. If there is an NDP infiltration in these homes, it has to be stamped out.
That is the only way you will beat us in St. John's West.

I managed to keep the rot from spreading there in 1976 and I hope to keep the rot from spreading again this year.
Quite seriously, there is a lot of dissatisfaction with the condition of these homes. They are not as bad as the homes in
