the area which the hon. member for St. John's East is complaining about, and rightly so.
Might I make a suggestion to the minister, Mr. Chairman. One of the things that CMHC and the minister has stated to my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East, is that they cannot do anything. In my friend's case this gentleman incorporated a company to do the project. The project is now finished. There are no assets left in the company. The people in the development have been left with inferior homes. These homes are in Virginia Park in St. John's East. There is not much good these people suing the company which built the homes because the company is now only a shell. This well-known contractor in St. John's has now moved on to other projects. CMHC say, "Well, you can only follow your legal remedies." The legal remedies in this case are not much good to you. What is the good of suing a company with no assets?
Apart from the question whether CMHC should be held responsible, which I am sure my learned friend and colleague will deal with again, this contractor is also accused of having bribed a CMHC inspector. The way to deal with him is quite simple. CMHC should advise that contractor that if he does not put those homes in good repair and does not correct the deficiencies, never again will he or any company in which he is a shareholder, or in which any of his family are shareholders, or anyone found to be representing him, receive any financial assistance for a building project from CMHC. That is the least that CMHC can do to put some pressure on the contractor.
A contractor should not be allowed to use CMHC financing facilities unless his main company, his principal company, his head company, his company that has assets, guarantees the job. In other words, Joe Smith, whose main company is Smith Construction Ltd., should not be allowed to incorporate XYZ Construction Ltd. to do a job, such as the Virginia Park job, does that job only, and then comes back to CMHC with another incorporated company, without assets, and does a further job, and so on. In my opinion, in every case his main company should have to guarantee the work he has done to CMHC and to the purchasers of those homes. He should not be allowed to use the legal device.
The ordinary home buyer is an innocent party who will probably only buy a home once in his lifetime. People do not know what to look out for. When you talk about an AHOP unit, they are the lower income people who probably do not want to pay lawyers' fees or they think the CMHC lawyer is acting for them. But he is not acting for them unless they agree to pay him the usual fairly substantial legal fee. In this case where the government is involved, the old principle of caveat emptor has to be forgotten. It is not a case of "let the buyer beware". In this case the government is involved and it has to help the purchaser be aware. It is the government's responsibility. They are financing these kinds of developments. If they are trying to help low income families get houses, it is the government's responsibility to hold them by the hand as they go into these projects. In this case it was the government's responsibility to assist them as they bought the houses. If it turned out they had a bad bargain, that they had been put
Housing
upon as has happened in my friend's district, it is the government's responsibility to help them get out of that situation. It is not enough to say they will give them an increased loan to pay the thousands of dollars they have to pay to repair the monstrous conditions they are now experiencing.
I suggest that if CMHC investigates Kilbride and finds that there is poor workmanship, that people are having lots of problems there, CMHC should put pressure on the contractor in those developments. The contractor will not go back now with these individual complaints. The only way he will go back is if he gets extra legal pressure put on him. How can people who are barely able to cover their shelter costs because they are in an AHOP project hire lawyers to sue on their behalf if they need a few thousand dollars worth of repairs done? This is CMHC's program and it should help those who need help, but instead of helping them they have got them in over their heads. They have them tied to a mortgage which they have to repay and they are now leaving them to like it or lump it by themselves. That is not good enough. We are hoping that the minister will have some answers in this connection as this committee goes on.
I have another matter to bring up. I was not here this morning but I would like the minister to explain Mr. Hession's letter of January 3, 1979. The RRAP program has been very popular in Newfoundland particularly in my friend's district of St. John's East and in my district. It has been much used in the NIP areas there and in other areas. The people have been led by the minister to believe that RRAP is available now to them all. I used to write CMHC and ask them if they would include St. Mary's Bay as a RRAP designated area, Come-By-Chance and various other areas. Now it is universal, the minister says.
Mr. Hession's letter of January 3 to the minister certainly shows that that is not a correct statement. He said that the 1979 capital budget is $56 million and that $37 million has to be used in the existing designated areas where work has already begun. That leaves a further $3 million in areas already designated but where work has not started. That is $40 million. This leaves $16 million for new initiatives for the whole of 1979. He goes on to say that 68 areas have submitted final applications under the old rules. After this legislation is passed they can be designated by order in council and they have to have priority. They will require $7 million, which leaves $9 million to cover some 2,250 units. That is the universal amount.
As Mr. Hession says, this is a fairly modest amount and we should avoid raising expectations which we cannot satisfy. I say that the minister has roused expectations throughout this nation that he cannot satisfy, unless he is going to rise here this afternoon and say that he now has $600 million or $1 billion for this program.
We are not going to allow him to fool the people of Canada into thinking it is universal when according to his own president he has $9 million for the whole of Canada outside the

March 9, 1979
Housing
present RRAP areas and he can do 2,250 units during 1979. The people from St. Mary's Bay are going to hear from me, as well as the people from Placentia Bay and the people of St. John's West. Anybody who can hear my voice over the media, or in fact across the nation, every householder from the tip of St. John's East-if the hon. member does not mind me referring to his district-to Vancouver Island, will hear from me that this is not a universal program.
This is a universal fraud, a universal attempt at deception. A statue should be raised to our housing critic, Lady Pigott, the member for Ottawa-Carleton who exposed this massive attempt at deception by giving the world the letter from Mr. Hession. We are going to send Mr. Hession's letter to every householder in this country once the election is called. At least, if we do not, we should. The threat of it alone will be enough to strike fear into the heart of the minister because he will have to explain to the people in our areas who want to get loans and grants to repair their homes why they cannot get them when the program is now universal.
Mr. Hession went on to say:
You realize I am sure that neither the industry nor the municipal delivery system nor the present and projected RRAP budget permit the operation of a universal program in the specific sense that anyone, any day of the week can walk into a municipal office and be served.
He points out that he proposes a ten-year program to do 200,000 dwellings for those in the most serious need. He points out that two million could use the program. We have to go into that with the minister and try and get that straightened out.
I -want the minister to explain to me all about his speech to HUDAC on February 9 of this year. I said the other night that the minister was a wizard of weasel wording. He was going to bring in a great new program. We heard the Prime Minister admit here this morning that they do not have a thing to tinkle in. They could not even tinkle in the pot, they were so tight for money, except for the $18 million that the "minister of amateur fitness and professional sport" is talking about for NHL teams.
This minister said in his speech to HUDAC that our proposal for mortgage interest deductions was unsatisfactory and Canada would be better served by a tax credit scheme so that the new advertising campaign could start. Where did the money come from, honey? All we know is it came from the government. Where does the government get the money, honey? The government gets the money from us, honey.
That is the most dishonest advertising program since Mr. Smallwood left the political scene. They have brought themselves finally to the Smallwood level. I never thought I would see the day when anybody could be lower in that regard than our former premier, but I have seen it now.
You are doing pretty well yourself.
You get on your feet and we'll be delighted to hear you.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member has invited me to get on my feet if I have anything to

say. I simply said, in case he did not understand me, that he is doing pretty well himself to bring someone down to the Smallwood level. In fact, I think he has surpassed that level in depth.

I will pass on the good wishes of that Liberal member to Mr. Smallwood, who will probably get his tongue around him if he ever goes to Madawaska. I am going to ignore the interjection from the gnats and the mosquitos in the Liberal party. We are only interested in the horse flies and the horse dragons, not in the little buzzers, only the large ones.
The minister had this to say:
To introduce any general program, however, that seeks to redistribute income for shelter purposes, requires a very substantial commitment of government funds. As a minister of the government in power, I do not have the advantage of being able to advocate prodigality on the one hand and retrenchment and restraint on the other.
I asked the other night why this minister is being discriminated against. Why is he the only minister of the government that is not allowed to promise more spending on one hand and less on the other? Every other minister does it. Why is he discriminated against? The minister went on to say:
But I do believe that in the near future, as soon as our economy permits, we should adopt a shelter allowance system that will provide assistance to home owner and tenant alike, through payment of a tax credit for shelter expenditures exceeding a certain percentage of income.
Before this bill clears the House, the minister should tell the people of Canada when he is going to introduce that program. He should put a date on it. Can the minister tell us when the economy is going to permit his great new program? When is he going to be able to bring it in and what are the details?
What is the point of the minister saying there is going to be a program if the promise is that it is going to be brought in as soon as our economy permits? The minister knows that as long as his government is in power the economy is never going to permit the bringing in of such a program.
We are promising the people of Canada that mortgage interest and municipal tax deductibility will be brought in as soon as we are brought in. When the people of Canada bring us in, they are bringing that program in with us. The people of Canada have had this government for 15 years and it has not yet introduced this program to redistribute income for shelter purposes or a shelter allowance system. They have been here 15 or 16 years and now the minister says that some time in the future, as soon as the economy permits, he is going to bring it in.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may speak again after someone else has spoken.

Mr. Chairman, in the traditional spirit of co-operation that characterizes our Friday afternoon sittings, I am glad to see that the minister is in an unusually good and co-operative mood. He was, however, uncharacteristically brief and we had to prompt him to say a few opening words on clause 1 of the bill notwithstanding the practice that it is customary on clause 1, when we are in committee of the whole
March 9, 1979

or in standing commmittee, for the minister to make a statement.
In that same co-operative spirit, the same born again spirit that I perceive in the minister-he sits there smiling at me-I still have hope the minister will address himself to some of the problems that we raised during second reading stage of the bill and which have been repeated here today on clause 1 of the bill by my colleagues.
I have a special interest because of the constituents I have the honour to represent in this House, those unfortunate people caught by a bureaucratic kind of stalemate with regard to the Virginia Park AHOP development. That case has been made in this House. It has been made outside the House by the solicitor for the AHOP home owners in Virginia Park. The minister has correspondence on it. I will not repeat all that I said on second reading. I am not going again to lay the whole horror story on the record because that would be taking advantage of the committee.
I am firm in my resolve that this matter has to be addressed. There has to be some indication from the minister before this debate ends that the government is going to live up to the responsibility that it assumed on behalf of these home owners when it agreed to extend financing under the National Housing Act and the assisted home ownership plan to the builder, who is now no longer in business because he conveniently put together a paper company for the purpose of building this sub-development.
The minister nods his head. I find that encouraging. I am not going to belabour the point. I take the minister at his word. He says he is going to tell us when we get to clause 3. Why cannot he tell us on clause 1 ?
The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock has outlined the problems in his constituency in the Vancouver area. The hon. member for Hamilton has outlined similar problems in his own area. We could go within a mile of the minister's own constituency in Montreal and find AHOP projects where there are problems which seem to characterize AHOP programs all across the country. There has been a spirit of give and take evident in the last few days. I must admit I do not know who is taking; we can never be sure in that regard, and I do not say this unkindly but in reference to the hon. gentleman's sharpness as a politician.
It seems to me we have reached a productive arrangement as a result of which when the bill before us is on third reading it will in many respects be a vast improvement on that which we dealt with on second reading. But in the interests of making progress I hope the minister will state what are the intentions of the corporation with respect to the AHOP home owners in Virginia Park, in the constituency of my hon. friend from St. John's West, in the Hamilton area and in the Surrey area.
If he does not, then out of the sense of support that I feel for the people we represent I cannot promise we will make the kind of progress we would all like to see. After all, this is the only chance I have to make a case in this House on behalf of
Housing
those unfortunate low income people who bought these houses with the guarantee of the corporation, knowing that they had the backing of the National Housing Act and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. So I invite the minister to tell the committee now what he is prepared to do about these home owners, not only in St. John's but elsewhere in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks on clause 1 were very brief. I felt that because there were before us a series of amendments dealing with a number of points which have been presented by members of the opposition it would be more appropriate for me to address those points specifically as each of the amendments came before the committee. However, I respect the view expressed by the hon. member for St. John's East, who has invited me to address myself specifically to the difficult situation in whith home owners in Virginia Park and certain other AHOP projects in various places in Canada find themselves.
One of the amendments presented later today will be introduced by the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton. Under its terms, we would enshrine in the National Housing Act a clause which would provide that, in the case of a loan made to a builder for the purpose of house construction, the builder should provide the purchaser with a warranty under a warranty program approved by the corporation.
There is no doubt in our minds that in future no loans should be insured by CMHC unless the builder offers a warranty program to the purchaser. I want to remind hon. members that I have been advocating this for a long time. As a former minister for consumer and corporation affairs I made many speeches advocating such a program, so one of the first things I did when I was appointed minister responsible for urban affairs was to discuss with the National Association for Housing and Urban Development the desirability of setting up a warranty program. We presently have a national warranty program which is administered by each provincial association. In practice, though, CMHC no longer insures loans for building projects unless such projects carry a guarantee to the purchaser. I am glad to note that the hon. member wants to enshrine this practice in the National Housing Act. I support her initiative and hope the House will approve the amendment.
In relation to the case which has been put forward in the House in recent weeks by the hon. member for St. John's East on behalf of some of his constituents who have been very badly affected by the incidents in Virginia Park, I told him in the House that the tools at our disposition were very limited but that CMHC was acknowledging the difficulties these people were facing. I assured him we were ready to put up the cash money required to enable them to carry out the necessary repairs immediately but that CMHC had no authority to make grants to these people. There is no provision allowing CMHC to do this. But we are ready to make an advance to them, to re-open their AHOP files and give them an appropriate amount of money with which to pay for these necessary repairs, and to make appropriate arrangements with the individuals concerned for reimbursement to be spread out over as long a period as possible.

March 9, 1979
Housing
Also, there were certain grants attached to the old AHOP program. I know that in Virginia Park some of the residents have an income which is sufficiently low to allow them to benefit from such grants in relation to the offer made by CMHC. I would be quite willing to re-open each individual file in order to help them. The response by the hon. member at the time was that something more had to be done and that some specific adjustments had to be made for these people.
After consultations with the representatives of these people I would be prepared to appoint someone to act as a special adviser to CMHC and to these people, to make recommendations in order to solve the problem of these residents. I recognize the difficulties which are inherent in these actions. At the risk of going beyond the legal responsibility of CMHC I think we ought to take an affirmative step which would allow these people to receive some relief, but not under the legal umbrella. I understand that they have lawyers who have put their case before the court. Perhaps through the court they will receive a much more substantial remedy than they could expect at this moment, but I am ready and willing, without prejudice to their court claim, to appoint a special mediator or ombudsman to deal specifically with their case, to re-open their file and to try to accommodate them quickly so that the problems they have at the present time can be solved.
The errors of the past ought to be corrected, and the ideal way to do that is to make sure that no loan is insured by CMHC unless the builder guarantees the purchaser that there is a warranty plan to protect him.
The second thing I want to say is that indeed, as suggested by the hon. member for St. John's West, I am ready to develop guidelines within the CMHC for dealing in the future with the builders of these projects about which there are complaints. I want to assure the hon. member that we on this side of the House are no more happy-and we are probably as disappointed and disgusted as the hon. member-than the hon. member about some of these things which have taken place in the past. Indeed, we do not approve of the conduct of builders who create companies just for the purpose of financing one project, after which those companies immediately disappear. They escape any liability or responsibility. I am ready to say to the hon. member for St. John's West that we will develop guidelines to make sure that CMHC will not in future do business with those companies which have bad records.

Mr. Chairman, there are a couple of questions I would like to put to the minister. I am especially interested in the community services program proposal in this legislation. It was announced last May, and a number of municipalities in my constituency have been especially concerned about when these funds will actually be made available. Some of them applied for funding for projects under the four programs which where amalgamated into the community services program. I understand that about $51 million is available for the province of Ontario in the first year, and larger amounts in subsequent years. That would be out of $150 million the first year and

$250 million the second year for the whole country. I would like to know how soon this agreement with the province of Ontario will be implemented.
I am thinking especially of communities like Sault Ste. Marie, where a large sewage treatment facility and water mains are to be installed. There is also a neighbourhood improvement project to be developed. I am thinking also of communities like Little Current, which is putting in a sewer and water system. It applied for funding last year. The project did not get under way in 1978, so the community is waiting to know how soon that funding will be committed so that it can go ahead with tendering on the project. There has been approval from the province of Ontario, but funds under this program have not actually been identified.
I am also thinking of the community of Elliot Lake, which is growing very rapidly. There are some 15,000 people there now, and the community will grow to over 30,000 in the next four or five years. There is a very rapid expansion of infrastructures such as sewer and water. A community like that really has to know from where funding will be coming. Indeed, it will require all available assistance under the community services program, from the Ontario department of the environment, as well as assistance under a subsidiary agreement with DREE, because of the massive funding which will be necessary. That is one matter I wanted to put to the minister. How soon will agreement with the province of Ontario be reached? Time is marching on, and if contracts are to be let for construction this year, that has to be done very soon.
The second matter I want to raise with the minister is whether there can be some special assistance under the rental supplement program for communities like Elliot Lake which are growing very rapidly. In such communities mining companies subsidize the rents of their employees. For a new housing unit which would cost $55,000, $60,000 or $65,000, the rent would normally be about $400, but the mining company would charge only $200. That is fine for the employees of the mining company, but there are people who work in the service sector who do not have that kind of assistance, so it seems to me that there has to be some mechanism developed for communities which are expanding very rapidly. That mechanism should provide proper accommodation for people in the service sector. It seems to me that a rental supplement program is the only solution for medium and lower income families.
I am familiar with one problem regarding the rental supplement program which is carried out jointly with the Ontario government. If a project is developed by the private sector, I think normally only one quarter of the units can be eligible for this rental supplement, and I wonder if in fact there is enough leeway in this legislation, or in the National Housing Act, to allow for entire apartment blocks or housing complexes to be set up so that there would be this rental supplement but not restricted just to one quarter of the units. I would be very interested in knowing if the minister feels that that kind of assistance could be made available to Elliot Lake, where approximately 3,000 units will be developed over the next few
March 9, 1979

years to accommodate expanding uranium production at that community.
I hope the minister will be able to respond to those two questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will answer the questions raised by the hon. member very quickly. In the first place 1 would like to say that 1 have had preliminary discussions with representatives of the Ontario government. They have already submitted their documents for signature. We expect to sign an agreement with the government of Ontario dealing with the community services program. As soon as this bill is passed, we hope to have the signatures some time next week.
In relation to the second point raised by the hon. member, indeed, under section 44(1 )(a) and 44(1 )(b) of the National Housing Act we have an agreement with the government of Ontario to designate four supplementary subsidies when the province decides to designate these units. So rent supplements could be granted to specific projects that the hon. member has in mind. It would be up to the Ontario government to designate these units, and the federal government would then be willing to accept this and pay the rent supplement on a 50-50 basis with the Ontario government.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to be seen to be intervening more than is reasonable and necessary, but I did not take up my time because I wanted the minister to reply to my invitation to him to respond to clause 1 to the grievances that I put forward on second reading on behalf of the people of Virginia Park. I want to say to the minister that I believe the proposal he has put forward is, under the circumstances, a reasonable one.
The people I have the honour to represent, the home owners in Virginia Park, are reasonable, decent, honest, hard working people, and they believe in the justice of their case, so much so that they, with great personal expense to themselves, engaged solicitors and consulting engineers because they believe their case is just and will stand in any court of justice or any tribunal. That is why I say to the minister that I welcome his suggestion to appoint an arbitrator, a mediator, or an ombudsman who would act independently between both parties, the CMHC on the one side and the Virginia Park home owners on the other. I know that that suggestion will be welcomed by these people.
This prompts me to make another suggestion, one which I have cleared with my colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton, who should be commended on the very forthright manner in which she has handled this bill, and indeed on the way she has addressed herself to the whole problem of the housing industry and the impact on the economy and the way it affects individual Canadians. This brings me to a suggestion which 1 would like to put to the minister. Most major corporations in the country today which deal with the public have a vice president or a senior executive who deals with consumer affairs or consumer relations, someone who handles specifical-
Housing
ly consumer complaints at an executive level. There is no such person within CMHC. I think the experience of the Virginia Park home owners demonstrates the need for such a senior officer within CMHC, a practice that has been widely and effectively used by most of the major corporations dealing with the public in commercial transactions.
I know I cannot put this forward as an amendment beause it carries with it a charge against the Treasury, and so the amendment would not be procedurally acceptable. I can only make it as a suggestion. I put it forward to the minister, safe in the knowledge that with his background as former minister of consumer and corporate affairs and with the way he has responded to the complaints we have raised in the House on behalf of my constituents, of Virginia Park home owners, and others as well, I know that this is a suggestion he will not treat lightly. I hope it is one which the corporation will accept and that, before long, we will have such an official appointed within CMHC.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext: I want to say that this is a very worthy suggestion, and indeed with my previous experience in consumer affairs I welcome the suggestion. I will be speaking with the chairman of the board of CMHC, with the recommendation that appropriate procedures be applied to have one of the vice presidents of CMHC pay particular attention to consumer matters.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make some comments in three areas. I restrained myself on second reading from making a speech, and now I will try to be brief in commenting on the three areas. I hope I will receive some answers from the minister in these areas.
The first one has to do with native housing. Some years ago the announcement was made that some 50,000 structures will be built for natives in, I believe, seven years. At the moment, a little over 7,000 have been built. When I look at the statistics on what is happening on reserves, I find that much still needs to be done. The statistics come from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and I will read a couple pertaining to a few of the provinces. We find that reserve Indian families needing homes in Ontario number 2,270 out of 7,000 families which still have no place in which to live. In Quebec, 1,182 families out of 4,353 families have no place to live. In the province of Alberta, 662 out of 2,821 families have no place to live. These families are living on reserves with their parents and brothers, or in rental accommodation together with a number of other families.
In the province of Alberta, the province with which I am most familiar, in the last couple of months-I am not sure exactly how many-some babies died from respiratory problems, and the Indian people in that area put the total blame for those deaths on inadequate housing. It was documented on television and in the newspapers that, in the mobile home where one of the babies died, three families, or 16 or 17 people, resided, a mobile home with the space for only one family or three or four people. At present they are documenting hundreds of more cases in northern Alberta living in
COMMONS DEBATES	March 9, 1979
Housing
similar conditions. The native people in the province consider housing to be the number one priority.
I am fortunate in my riding to have two reserves which have oil money available for their use, and the first area for which they have designated royalties from their oil is the building of homes on the reserves. But by far the greatest number of native people in Alberta are not as lucky and they require assistance in housing from the federal government, and the total responsibility should be on the federal government for giving assistance in housing to the native people.
Under RRAP, money can be made available for native housing, and not only on reserves, because this problem is now extending itself to the cities of this country as young people and families from the reserves are moving to the cities in an attempt to find jobs and get off the welfare rolls and off the unemployment insurance rolls. So we must look at the problem as not only a problem on the reserve but also as a problem in the cities of our nation.
Under this program as well, it is possible to provide assistance for the repair of homes. The statistics tell me-in the non-native community we would never put up with such a situation-that only 80 per cent of native houses have electricity, only 31 per cent have water and sewage facilities, only 30 per cent have indoor toilets, only 26 per cent have indoor baths, and less than a third have telephones. Surely we in the non-native community would not put up with such housing conditions, and I do not think that we, as Canadians, should accept that the native people have to live in that way either.
I see that under this program it is possible to make conversions and major repairs to dwellings, and I hope that the minister will say that certain funds will be set aside under this program for this purpose. Perhaps the minister could tell us how many more homes out of the 50,000 can be built in the next number of years, and whether some funds can be provided under RRAP for the repair of homes and the building of new homes. I would like to spend a lot of time on that, but I realize our time in committee is limited and I want to deal with another area. That other area is the CHIP insulation program.
When it was announced, people who owned older homes felt that the program would provide them with a method of reducing their fuel bills. According to an announcement, I believe some 900,000 dwellings were available for the program, that is, homes built before 1946. For some reason the program has failed. Approximately $65 million was set aside for the program, and it has not been spent. The statistics in Alberta indicate that there are 120,000 homes built prior to 1946 which are eligible for the program, and that only 2,200 grants have been given out in that province.
I had occasion to speak with the chap in charge of the program in Alberta. He indicated that because of the surplus of gas in that province, Albertans are not concerned about insulating their homes. I do not believe that. Anyone who can save on his heating bill will take advantage of it; it does not
[Mr. Schellenberger.J
matter from which province he comes. I could cite similar statistics for other provinces, but I will deal only with my own.
For some reason the program was not put properly before Canadians. Possibly it was because the $350 grant was taxable and many people felt it was not worth going through the problems of receiving the grant. I understand that major recommendations have been approved within the department to change the program somehow. I have a letter from the Insulation Contractors Association of Ontario. I will not read it, but it indicates that changes must be made in order for the association to take advantage of the program and insulate thousands of homes within Ontario. They are looking forward to the changes which the minister is capable of announcing in the very near future. Perhaps he can make such an announcement today, or perhaps he can make it as soon as possible if such recommendations have been approved within his department. If not, I suggest a long look should be taken at this program.
Until one o'clock this morning I was in the energy committee which was dealing with the energy allocations bill. According to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, there is a crisis respecting the allocation of oil, particularly in eastern Canada. The best way to save on our energy requirements is by conservation. This program should be successful and should do Canadians a great deal of good, yet it is failing.
Earlier this year an announcement emanated from CMHC regarding the addition of solar panels in homes. I am not sure of the person's name who wrote an article dealing with this matter, but I believe he suggested that people who feel there is some future in putting solar panels in their homes can be compared to zealots. I simply cannot accept such a remark coming from people within CMHC. This is an area which the Canadian government must move into in order to provide renewable energy for Canadians who are willing to take the chance and put solar panels in their homes. The technology is there, but it requires CMHC assistance by allowing mortgages to be extended at least ten years to 15 years in order for home owners to pay off the costs of the installation of solar equipment in their homes. I hope the minister is looking at this and is in a position to give some answers respecting those three areas.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member for Wetaskiwin I should like to indicate that the rural and native housing program started a few years ago. It has provided approximately 18,000 units out of the target of 50,000 units which we wanted to do over a course of five years to seven years. The reason why the start has been slow and that we have not produced a larger number of units is because we want to involve natives in the program. We want their input into the implementation of it. Of course we were ready to suffer some delay in the implementation of the program because we felt it would be useful for them to be part and parcel of such a program. Our average in production every year is now good, and we believe we will meet the target of 50,000 units.
In relation to the hon. member's second point, I agree the CHIP program perhaps did not receive the response we
March 9, 1979

expected from the public at large. It is an important program, but we still have a job to do in convincing Canadians that they could be very active in the conservation of energy. One of the best ways for Canadians to be active is for them to insulate their homes and spend the necessary moneys to have well-insulated homes. Indeed it would be a wise investment because, in the long run, their heating bills will be reduced. In order to provide an extra incentive in that regard, we have put forward a program to give $350 to home owners in order for them to insulate their pre-1946 homes. Discussions are taking place perhaps to improve some aspects of the program. In relation to the dates, recommendations were made to the effect that now that the old stock has had a chance to benefit from the program, maybe more recent housing stock should be eligible as well. I am looking at this proposal, and I hope to reach a decision soon.
In relation to the hon. member's third point, I agree fully that it is an area to which we must give much more attention in the future, and I support his view on it.

Mr. Chairman, before we proceed with clause by clause consideration, the minister suggested that he will appoint an ombudsman. I would like to have this clarified. Is that to look into just the situation in Virginia Park, or is he saying that he will have an ombudsman to look into these situations wherever and whenever they occur? This party takes the position that there is increasing evidence that the cost of land is one of the primary elements in housing inflation and has been one of the primary elements in the extraordinary housing inflation in Canada since the mid-1960s. We also take the view that land assembly should remain one of the critical features of the policy of any government that is determined to do something about profiteering in land speculation and the increasing conditions of monopoly in the assembly of land that we see in Canada today.
We are political realists, if nothing else, and we accept the fact that the government has rejected this view and has taken a view that the return to the so-called free market in the assembly of land will provide the best protection for the Canadian public. I think that view is completely misplaced, but it seems to be the view of the government.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. There have been consultations and I believe it is unanimously agreed that you not see the clock for the next 25 minutes or so in order that we complete this stage of the bill. I think there is unanimous agreement.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make quite clear our position on the graduated payment mortgage scheme. The position that our party has taken consistently has been that there is a need for a home ownership assistance program, but that this is a phony solution to a very serious problem.
The graduated payment mortgage scheme in fact creates a higher level of debt for the individual and his family than would otherwise be the case in taking out an equal payment mortgage, the kind of mortgage most people have. It is an attempt to sugar the very unpleasant pill of inflated mortgage payments and inflated interest rate payments. It is not a solution to that problem.
The position of this party has been that rather than allow the banks to pick up profits at the expense of people on the basis of a government policy of having a high interest rate, and their profits are nearly $ 1 billion, we should be instructing the lending institutions to begin providing lower mortgage rates for families below a certain level of income. That deals with the problem of interest rates directly, not indirectly as this does. It does not saddle people with a higher level of debt than they can afford.
The premise upon which the whole concept of graduated payment mortgages is based is twofold. The first premise is that inflation will increase the value of the house automatically. The second premise is that incomes will continue to increase and the level of income of a family will be constant and will increase over time.
Both those assumptions are false and very dangerous. There is no telling what inflation will do to the value of a house or what it will do to the value of a house relative to the cost of living. The fact is that in the past two years the rate of inflation has surpassed the increase in the value of existing housing stock.
The second premise on which it is based is equally false. It is that we are going to have guaranteed employment for both wage earners in the family and that those people will be working at a higher level of income five years from now. That is a false premise. With the nature of the economy which has been created and encouraged by this government, we know that there is an increasing prospect of unemployment amongst men and women, that families can no longer rely on two salaries in order to pay the GPM, and that people will not necessarily be able to afford the kinds of payments required by the GPM scheme.
I know that the headlines say this is a home ownership program designed to help young families purchase homes. The

minister's public relations are very good. I congratulate him on them. However, the press should look very carefully at the hard facts as to exactly what this kind of scheme will cost individuals as compared to existing schemes. Compare what it would cost an individual if we had the courage in this country to take on the lending institutions and told them to lower their interest rates. There is no comparison.
Instead of going around the circle of the problem and attempting to make high interest rates more palatable to people, the government should be determined to hold down interest rates and, in fact, lower the rate of interest. In our view that is the best, most effective, and most honest way to get hold of the problem of mortgage payments for young people.
Mr. Chairman, I want to underscore what has been said by my new friend from Broadview-
Socialist!

His comments are well taken. I do not necessarily agree with the solutions he offers but he was certainly able to identify with the problem. I want to underscore that GPMs can work only if they are applied to families with high income mobility. This is where they have been successful. They are not a financing instrument to be used for low income Canadians. Let it be clearly known that we in the Progressive Conservative party do not endorse the scheme in such circumstances though we recognize it as being a useful tool in the case of families with high income mobility. What I would like to do is simply explain what the purpose of this amendment is with respect to the community service grants program. The community service grants program proposed by the government is part of its effort to appease the provinces and cut off its direct relationship with the municipalities. The community service grants program is not only intended to replace the neighbourhood improvement program as has been suggested by some people, it is intended to replace this program together with a vast number of other programs which I would like to list, including sewage treatment, trunk lines and plants, community water supply facilities, trunk storm sewer systems, sewer and water site services, social and cultural facilities, community recreational facilities, non-profit housing in municipal equity, upgrading and insulation of municipal buildings and community facilities, facilities which convert municipal waste to energy production and any municipal capital works specified in the federal-provincial operating agreement.
The complaint we have about this entire concept, is that the government, in getting out of this area and limiting its activities to giving a bloc fund to the provinces, will have the effect of cutting out the neighbourhood improvement programs. This is because the amount of money allocated by the federal government to the provinces will so quickly be absorbed by basic infrastructure expenditures. In other words, the money being spent on sewer systems and so on-the very important work of neighbourhood improvement which goes on in many of our urban centres-will simply go by the board and be taken over by the building of basic infrastructure. This is why we have opposed the entire concept of a community service grants program which, we say, will do nothing but bring to an end those neighbourhood improvement projects and those cultural and community recreational facilities which are so important to people living in our urban areas.
In our view it also represents a dangerous tendency on the part of the government to abandon important areas of jurisdiction-and I think they can be argued as being under federal jurisdiction-at a time when cities and communities are starved for funds and continue to look to the federal government for leadership and for assistance. The federal government is cutting those groups off and saying, "Nothing doing, boys, you can go back to the provinces." I think this is not only politically a very big mistake in that it means that people will no longer look to the federal government for leadership at a time when they should be able to do so, but philosophically, and at a social level, it represents an abandonment by the government of people living in our urban areas. I think it is a major mistake.

subtopic: SUGGESTED STUDY OF NEEDS IN MARITIME PROVINCES
SUGGESTED STUDY OF NEEDS IN MARITIME PROVINCES
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on Regional Development be empowered to study the concept of using transportation as a development tool by putting in place a modern transportation network in the Maritime provinces, incorporating bus, train, highway and air services, and report back to the House its Findings on the desirability and the best ways and means of achieving such a concept.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we must focus the attention of ail departments of government on the issue of regional development if we are to succeed in helping Canadians who live in the Atlantic provinces to help themselves. Transportation is of paramount importance to the region, and since it is related directly to the whole question of regional economic expansion I want it placed before the appropriate committee of this House to be considered and dealt with, within the total context of that committee's mandate.
Before I suggest that air transportation ban be improved in the maritime provinces, I have to tell the House that it is our best mode of transportation available at this point in time. The problem is that we do not have enough direct flights within the maritimes and between points in the maritimes and points in central Canada and northern parts of the United States. We do not have these flights because we do not have enough volume of trade to make them pay. Even with the large subsidies which are paid to air carriers, we still have difficulty in providing the numbers that are needed to make it a good, efficient operation.
The sad fact is that we are never going to have the numbers or the trade unless we first have the service, and therein lies the key to our basic problem in transportation in the Atlantic provinces. A high quality of air cargo service is absolutely essential if Atlantic Canada is to develop a good industrial and commercial base. In this regard some of the larger firms in the Atlantic provinces have purchased their own planes.
Rail passenger service and, to a degree, rail freight have not really been given a good chance in the Atlantic provinces because the railways have allowed their rail beds to deteriorate to the point where trains move very slowly, and the equipment they use, particularly with respect to passenger service, is generally 25 years of age or older. Depending heavily on the United States for reefer cars which the railways rent or buy, our potato industry has been affected detrimentally by the shortage of equipment.
The gateway to commerce in the maritimes is the deep water ports of Halifax and Saint John which, because of their advantageous geographic position, can become arteries of commerce in an expanding trade environment if the ports are properly equipped with modern facilities. Improved terminal storage and handling facilities are badly needed in the Atlantic provinces.
Highways in the Atlantic provinces are the principal arteries of commerce and they are carefully preserved by our highway

March 9, 1979
Maritime Transportation
departments. Highway weight restrictions are essential in the spring to preserve the roads for use during the balance of the year. This means, of course, that truckers have to operate with limited loads and therefore make more runs to achieve the same volume of traffic, which adds considerably to the cost of transporting goods.
The economy can be stimulated by an improved highway network. Four lane highways can be built in many instances on existing rights of way, and with two lanes going in each direction, turn and elevation gradients require less expense to permit safe passage than is the case with single lane roads. This significant saving would go a long way toward paying for the additional pavement.
These more modern highways are not as much in evidence in the maritimes as they should be because, without federal aid, our provincial governments have not the funds to build them. In New Brunswick, for example, I feel the federal government should participate financially in a ring road around Fredericton, the new highway bridge across the river at Fredericton, and a four lane highway connecting Fredericton, the capital city, with the port of Saint John.
When approached with such concepts, the federal government is only too quick to suggest that current traffic needs do not warrant such expenditures. New Brunswick's five-year highway and bridge program which contained such a concept was discouraged by this government only two years ago. The point I am making is that the traffic will never warrant such highways unless the highways are built to stimulate development and thus develop the population that would warrant the highways.
Despite all the subsidies, freight rates remain too high because they are too high to begin with. We had a good example of this before the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications on May 31, 1977, in reference to our very important New Brunswick forest products. A comparison was made between the rates in New Brunswick and in British Columbia, and on raw wood products we found that rates in New Brunswick were 60 per cent higher.
Instead of paying increasing freight rates to ship our farm produce to distant markets and buying back cooked meats, bottled jams and canned vegetables, we urgently need a fun-damenal change in our transportation and DREE policies to enable us to develop plants to purchase and process local products in New Brunswick for sale in New Brunswick and across Canada, and, through tariff changes, to our natural trading partners along the Atlantic seaboarb. We have the resource potential to supply and operate plants to process cheese, meats, fruits and vegetables, to name only a few. I urge the government to invest in the future of New Brunswick and to take this giant step in creating good jobs and markets for our farming community. My remarks apply equally to Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.
The simple concept that we must ask ourselves in terms of transportation cost is, "How much does it cost to get a product to market economically? How much does it cost to get it there now?" Any difference in cost must demand a subsidy, or a roll

back in freight rates. A user-pay concept cannot achieve this purpose.
The railways should be required to retain, modernize and upgrade the service they presently give to the total area of the maritimes. Better rail freight cars are absolutely essential for shippers, particularly for agricultural products, and the integration of rail freight and passenger service with other forms of transportation is an important step in developing an efficient transportation system.
The federal government should not simply content itself with giving a department such as DREE a limited degree of authority. It should establish machinery which would produce co-ordinated results and which would, in terms of regional economic development, co-ordinate the policies of all departments, particularly, transport and finance, with the policies being followed by DREE.
I cannot emphasize too strongly the importance of coordinating efforts within departments of the federal government. It is also necessary to co-ordinate the efforts of the federal and provincial governments, especially in the Atlantic region. The three maritime provinces have improved their machinery for interprovincial co-operation, but we are still a long way from a plan of development for the region in which each provincial government and the federal would play a co-ordinating role.
DREE should get away from the idea that its main responsibility is to provide industrial incentives to entrepreneurs who wish to move into the Atlantic area, or to local businessmen who want to expand their present operations, or a series of ad hoc programs providing valuable services but on a small piecemeal scale. DREE should be doing far more than that. It should be looking hard at the big jobs crying to be tackled. For example, what has DREE done about the Fundy tidal power project? Nothing. It is very convenient for the government, whenever Fundy is seriously mentioned, to be able to pass it off to a study, or a commission, or a committee, which it knows full well can stall the project another year or another decade. Why is DREE not brought into these discussions? Why is not DREE handed the responsibility of correlating these studies? Why is not DREE given the job to do?
DREE was created to lead the attack on regional disparity. Like Uriah the Hittite, it was to be thrust into the forefront of battle, there to do or die. But DREE stayed in the background when the big conflicts raged. It handed out its grants and loans to justify its existence and failed miserably to take hold of the big projects which the Atlantic provinces have needed for generations. In short, it avoided the massive development undertakings without which the Atlantic provinces will always remain what they are today-the most neglected part of Canada.
I am an infrastructure man. I will always be an infrastructure man, for infrastructures are the only hope of getting Atlantic Canada into a position of parity with the rest of the country, a position from which it can stay caught up. Millions of dollars in piecemeal grants over the years have done nothing
March 9, 1979

but keep us from sliding farther behind, and that itself is an achievement. The dole has failed.
Now it is time to develop a bold and imaginative policy of regionalism, the principle of special aid to the Atlantic provinces on a massive scale-where mere millions have been parceled out to keep the wolf from the door, billions are needed; billions not in spending but in investment-investment in permanent and lasting projects which will bring the Atlantic provinces to equal-partner status with the other six, and which will dispose of the need, once and for all, of the subsidies and handouts which have always been associated with us as a backward area.
I believe that the infrastructures necessary for economic growth involve water, power, roads, railways, port facilities, sewers, schools, universities and research establishments, among others.
The provision of infrastructure should be an important part of the operations of DREE, which must launch a mighty drive to get the job done. DREE must have the powers to provide assistance by direct action, and by action through the provincial governments to create the necessary infrastructures.
DREE was launched with great fanfare as the answer to all of our economic problems. It did not take very long, however, for the Atlantic provinces to realize what DREE was-just another federal agency handing out grants and loans and doles and shirking the responsibility of getting to the fundamental problems of the area, of spearheading the mighty projects which common sense tells us must be the cornerstones of Atlantic prosperity-the Fundy tidal power project, the development of the ports of Saint John and Halifax, and an Atlantic transportation policy which would provide modern high speed highways to transport agricultural and forest products, parts for manufacturing industries, and other goods to world markets via the ports of Saint John and Halifax, and by land, air and rail to Canadian markets.
Development of the ports of Saint John and Halifax as major growth centres connected to all parts of the maritimes by modern transportation systems is basic to the development of our region. These two ports jut far out into the Atlantic and can receive the largest tankers in the world and offer a transportation facility to the whole Atlantic seaboard which is not blessed with such a natural advantage.
Not one of these projects came under the aegis of DREE. After nine years of DREE, the positions of each of these projects are exactly as they were when DREE was created-in limbo.
I believe that new policies should show a willingness to get to the basics of the Atlantic economics and to put first things first. There has to be a new set of priorities, and the projects I have mentioned have to be in the top echelons of those priorities.
On a New Brunswick note, I want DREE and New Brunswick to work out a five-year plan of highway development that will put in place a modern and efficient network and, among other things, study the concept of a north-south highway
Maritime Transportation
running from St. Andrews through Fredericton to Campbell-ton, connecting to other major arterial highways which lead to other New Brunswick centres. The study should consider not only the important transportation function but the potential of the highway in developing resources, recreation and tourism in the interior of the province.
I am receiving more and more support in my campaign for Atlantic infrastructures. Some of my colleagues have joined me. I would hope for the support of more of them; the support of all Atlantic members as well as that of the minister responsible for DREE. I am not asking for the moon. I am asking for fair treatment in an area with problems no amount of subsidies and grants can solve if a solid base is not laid down.
Give us the Fundy tidal project and the maritimes will become the powerhouse of the continent, with Canadian, American, British, French and Japanese interests clamouring to invest. Give us the modern highways, rail lines, bus and air systems, and the shippers, travellers and tourists will come to our area as we come in time closer to the markets and attractions of central Canada, and vice-versa. Give us the port developments, and the great tankers and container ships of the world will come to us in armadas of profit. In short, give us the infrastructures and let them form the foundation. Then the rest of Canada can forget the subsidies, grants and handouts which they have been forced to provide us, often against their will, for the simple reason no one has ever had the common sense, foresight and resolution to face facts squarely and give us the tools with which we can put our own house in order.
I want the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) to convene a meeting of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) with the premiers of all Atlantic provinces to devise a regional development strategy, to build modern infrastructure and identify areas of comparable natural advantage, committing the resources of our nation to develop them. Once we have a modern infrastructure in place and have identified the areas for regional development which should fit into a national industrial strategy, then we require the personal attention of the Prime Minister to focus the resources of our nation in a determined effort to develop the Atlantic provinces.
I thank the House for providing me with this opportunity by allowing private members' business to go forward this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to take part in the debate this afternoon as it provides me with an opportunity to set the facts straight. I just listened to the hon. member who spoke before me and who is a colleague from New Brunswick and in a certain way I think I am happy to be sitting on this side of the House rather than the other side, because he just gave us an absolutely exaggerated picture, a most gloomy picture not to say that he just put a host of half-truths on the record. So I

March 9, 1979
Maritime Transportation
would like to use the few minutes I have to set the record straight.

In participating in this debate on the motion presented by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie), let me first emphasize that DREE is very pleased to be able to discuss its role in the transportation sector of the maritime region. My government and I share the view that transportation is most important to the development of the maritime region, and that indeed the government, DREE in particular, has been and should continue to be very much involved in the important sector of transportation.
I should like to take the opportunity to quote some figures which speak for themselves. DREE has been in existence from 1969. The combined provinces of Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, under programs which have since concluded or under ongoing ones, have received in the field of transportation from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion a sum total of $353.5 million. DREE funds apply to the important infrastructure of transportation in the Atlantic area. My own province of New Brunswick has received its fair share under this program, the sum total of $118 million so far.
All hon. members now know that more programs are being negotiated and discussed. This is quite a record, and I am sorry the hon. member who has just sat down did not refer to DREE's involvement in the effort to improve the entire transportation structure in the Atlantic area.
I am not only referring to roads, paving, or roads to resources, but DREE has been involved in marine transportation. For example, it was involved in the Miramichi channel dredging study. It has been involved in port improvement facilities in Saint John. Contrary to what the hon. member has said, we are involved there on a continuing basis, and we are prepared to receive further submission from the province of New Brunswick. In spite of the fact that it is not its primary field of jurisdiction, DREE has become involved in airport construction in my riding. I am grateful to DREE for that contribution and participation, and I am looking forward to even greater participation.
There is no basis whatsoever for the hon. member to suggest that the government, DREE, and the Department of Transport, have not been involved seriously in ongoing discussions with the provinces. DREE has been involved even in fields which come under the primary jurisdiction of the provinces. DREE has gone into fields which have been the traditional reserve of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island because it is committed to improving the over-all infrastructure of Atlantic Canada since its establishment in 1969.
However, it appears that the motion proposed by the hon. member either reflects his lack of understanding of maritime transportation issues, or his lack of knowledge as to what DREE and the Department of Transport have been doing in this important area of endeavour. In the next few minutes I should like to tell the House of the work, planning, efforts, and the money which has been and indeed is being spent on transportation projects and undertakings in the maritimes by

DREE and the Department of Transport, so that it may be realized that the motion proposing "the Standing Committee on Regional Development be empowered to study the concept of using transportation as a development tool" in fact is inappropriate, redundant, and comes after action already is under way in the context of DREE's related efforts in the Atlantic region today. Also this is an opportunity to outline to hon. members the many initiatives taken by the Department of Transport to illustrate most clearly just how transportation is being used as a development tool in the Atlantic area. Many of these initiatives are a direct result of the consultative efforts of both federal and provincial officials and representatives of the private sector working together to improve the transportation system of the region at a time of severe restraint.
The hon. member has indulged in some local politics. He suggested that the federal government should share in the cost of the building of a bridge across a river in his riding. I think that is carrying it a little too far. There is a limit to what the federal government should be involved in with the provinces. Transportation, road transportation and bridge building, were and still very much are provincial responsibilities under the constitution. To want to drag the federal government into all phases of infrastructure building in the realm of their jurisdiction indeed is an exaggeration in the sense that these people are attempting to milk the federal cow to death.
Perhaps the best example of the fruits of our ongoing consultative process is the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Program announced almost two years ago in co-operation with provincial first ministers. This program was the result in part of a joint federal-provincial passenger transportation study embracing all modes. Subsequent to the study, a total of $125 million of Transport Canada money-this is above and beyond the figure I quoted just a few minutes ago of $350 million contributed by DREE-was allocated by the federal government for bus, highway and air services in the Atlantic provinces.
Surely the mere indication of those figures would indicate that the hon. member for York-Sunbury has not given the House the full story of the government's involvement in regional development in the maritime provinces, in New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, and certainly in Nova Scotia. As far as DREE is concerned, I would point out that important references to transportation are, indeed, enshrined in the General Development Agreements as negotiated by DREE on behalf of Canada with the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, as well as in the comprehensive development plan negotiated with Prince Edward Island.
In New Brunswick the general development agreement specifically recognizes the importance of the service sector to the province's economy, and pledges to implement a development strategy which will encourage the expansion of this sector. Transportation and distribution are cited as important components of New Brunswick's service sector. In Nova Scotia the general development agreement for that province specifi-
March 9, 1979

cally identifies distribution and transportation related industry as being of prime importance to the development strategy of that province.
The Prince Edward Island comprehensive development plan highlights the importance of adequate and reasonably priced transportation as an essential part of that province's developmental strategy. The plan also pledges to upgrade, where necessary, the island's network of resource collector and arterial roads and the feasibility of additional container service and other methods of moving freight are cited as worthy of joint study under the plan, as is the critical issue of the distribution of island potatoes and other bulk produce. That also applies to New Brunswick.
Both DREE and Transport Canada, in extremely close co-operation with provincial civil servants and politicians, have sat and studied these matters almost to the absurd. However, they did not stop at the study. They went ahead with a plan of action agreed to by all the parties. All the parties concerned are keeping an eye on the situation as it develops with a view to improving that infrastructure still more.
Through the general development agreements which were signed with the provinces, DREE has the mandate to pursue development opportunities in the maritime region in order to reduce the disparity gap. As it turns out, the general development agreement concept, with it's jointly agreed to strategy, is indeed proving to be a most flexible development tool to implement any indentified component of the region's transportation needs. Almost since its creation, DREE has worked with this important principle in mind. Indeed, prior to the general development agreement era, DREE was already involved in the construction of roads and highways under the FRED and ARDA programs in the special areas agreements.
There is a feature that I cannot help but notice every time I raise the question of transportation in my own Liberal caucus, because there are times when I must bring to the forefront and to the attention of the government some of the transportation problems of the Atlantic area, and that is when I hear my colleagues from British Columbia, western Canada, Ontario and parts of Quebec say, "How can you guys down in the maritimes muster so much government support?" On a per capita basis the maritimes indeed are being served much better than the rest of Canada from federal funds, to aid them in establishing needed and appreciated transportation infrastructures. I do not think that the maritimes should apologize for that federal help-far from me the thought. Far from me also is the thought that no work remains to be done.
Essentially what we are addressing here today is a reference to a committee to study the concept of using transportation as a development tool. What I am saying is that that concept has been very much in the mind of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and very much in the mind of Transport Canada. They have been co-ordinating committees at the interdepartmental level. There have been frequent meetings
Maritime Transportation
with provincial officials from all three provinces and they are being carried on on an ongoing basis, and there are federal-provincial management committees which meet regularly to review the progress being made on the transportation front.
I can come to no other conclusion than that the hon. member who posed this motion must be somewhat like Rip van Winkle and lived in a cave during this past decade.

After what he said I wonder if that is another one of the departments which the Progressive Conservative party will drop after the next election. They have committed themselves to dropping Petro-Canada, Loto Canada, and we now have a statement by an hon. member from that side that DREE should disappear altogether. That is incredible. I think that the hon. members on that side of the House should first consult with Premier Richard Hatfield who thought it a very advantageous position last fall to carry an election campaign based on the programs of DREE in his province.
I do not think, on the one hand, that they can say there has been close co-operation with the federal government, DREE and Transport Canada and, on the other hand, stand up in this House and pretend that we have unco-ordinated policies. As a New Brunswicker and maritimer I regret that negative approach. I am prepared to say that we may not have been successful on all fronts, but I do not think that we should be faulted for not trying, and the figures are certainly there to prove it.
